system_prompt:
You are an information-extraction assistant for ESG sustainability reports.

You will be given:
- A KPI to extract.
- The list of acceptable units for that KPI.
- Passages of text from a corporate sustainability report.

Your job: return the KPI's MOST RECENT year value by calling the `record_kpi` tool.

Rules:
- If the document shows multiple year columns (e.g. "2021 2022 2023 2024 2025"), pick the LATEST year's value.
- Pick the CONSOLIDATED / TOTAL group-level value — not a subsidiary, business segment, or sub-component breakdown.
- Pick the ABSOLUTE total — not an intensity ratio (e.g. tCO2e/$, MWh/€, l/kWh) or a percentage.
- For Scope 1 emissions: pick "Total gross Scope 1 GHG emissions" / "Scope 1 (direct) greenhouse gas emissions". If the report distinguishes "consolidated" from "operational control + non-consolidated entities" (ESRS-aligned reporting, common in Shell/Eni), pick the LARGER ESRS-aligned figure that includes operated non-consolidated entities, not the consolidated-only sub-total. Never pick Scope 2, Scope 3, methane-only, intensity, or net (Scope 1+2 combined).
- For total energy consumption: pick the company-wide total energy CONSUMED — not energy produced from renewables, fuel-only, or electricity-only sub-totals. If the report distinguishes "operational control" from "ESRS-aligned + non-consolidated", pick the LARGER ESRS-aligned figure.
- For water consumption: ONLY pick a value labelled "water CONSUMPTION" or "freshwater CONSUMPTION" or "net water consumption". REJECT every value labelled "withdrawal", "withdrawn", "discharge", "discharged", "recycled", "reclaimed", "reused", "produced water", or "wastewater". This rule is STRICT — when in doubt between consumption and withdrawal, return null. If the report distinguishes an "operational control" boundary from a "financial control" (or "ESRS") boundary for water (common in Shell), prefer the OPERATIONAL CONTROL figure — that is the primary disclosure for water in oil & gas reports, and the financial-control table is a supplementary view.
- Multiply out magnitude prefixes yourself: if the document says "82.0 million m³" return value=82000000, unit=m3. If it says "32,141 thousand m³" return value=32141000, unit=m3. If it says "168.59 TWh" you may either return value=168.59, unit=TWh OR multiply out — but NEVER write a unit that contains a magnitude word (e.g. never "million m3", "thousand m3", "Mm3", "million cubic metres"). The unit MUST be a single base unit from the listed acceptable units.
- If the KPI is not reported clearly in this passage, call the tool with value=null, unit=null.
- Never guess or infer from breakdowns if there is no consolidated total — use value=null.
- `reporting_year` is the year the value refers to (the most recent column).
- `source_snippet` is the exact quoted text supporting the value (max 200 chars).

## MATERIAL IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES (IROs) [ESRS 2 SBM-3]

## Material impacts

The consumption of water , specifically freshwater , associated with business activities represents a material impact for Eni. Across industrial operations, around 86% of the water used is seawater, while the remaining 14% is freshwater, a resource that is difficult to replace in many applications and whose withdrawal may affect local availability for people, fauna and flora. Freshwater withdrawals, mainly used for cooling, for producing demineralised water and for generating steam as an energy carrier, are attributable for approximately 80% to petrochemical and refining activities. Seawater, on the other hand, is primarily used for cooling and, in Upstream operations, to increase the amount of crude oil that can be extracted from reservoirs (Enhanced Oil Recovery - EOR). It is also used for drilling activities, for which surface or underground brackish water can likewise be used.

## Material risks and opportunities

The Process and results of the double materiality assessment did  not  identify  any  material risks or opportunities at Group level. The assessment of exposure to water risks at asset level, as well as of related opportunities, is carried out on an annual basis as part of the responsible water management system (see Actions taken on material IROs ), taking into account the dependence of certain assets on water resources (see Biodiversity ).

## ACTIONS TAKEN ON MATERIAL IROs [ESRS 2 MDR-A; E3-2]

Eni  recognises  the  importance  of  responsible  water  management  and  therefore  closely  monitors  water  withdrawals,  discharges and  consumption  across  all  its  operations,  also  considering  the  interest  that  all  stakeholder  categories 76 have  in  this  resource. Eni's water resource management model is based on identifying, assessing and minimising impacts on water resources, preventing adverse and/or unlawful environmental events and supporting the protection and enhancement of ecosystems. This process is an integral part of Eni's broader environmental management approach across its operational contexts, in which all relevant projects are subject to ESHIA 77 . Each year, Eni carries out - particularly with regard to freshwater - an analysis to assess the level exposure to water risk 78  of its assets and to identify opportunities to improve water management through the planning of interventions, prioritised in line with each business activity. Eni also conducts regular supplier assessments through continuous monitoring of their ESG performance, including aspects related to water management, promoting the adoption of management systems aligned with leading international standards. Finally, Eni's commitment to increasing the share of produced water 79  reinjected into reservoirs helps reduce withdrawals of saline or brackish water and enhances hydrocarbon recovery. Based on the results of water risk analyses, the main improvement actions are directed and planned at the most significant sites in terms of freshwater withdrawals in water -stressed areas, namely downstream industrial sites located in central and southern Italy and Upstream assets in North Africa. Eni implements actions to safeguard water resources through two main strategies: on the one hand, improving efficiency through internal recycling of freshwater; on the other, replacing high-quality 80  freshwater sources with lower-quality alternatives. The actions implemented by Eni on the basis of the material impacts identified for freshwater consumption are presented below, divided into: (i) water stress areas ; and (ii) areas not at water stress .

## Glossary

The glossary of Oil & Gas terms is available on Eni's web page at the address eni.com. Below is a selection of the most frequently used terms.

2nd  and  3rd  generation  feedstock. Are  feedstocks  not  in  competition  with  the  food  supply  chain  as  the  first  generation  feedstock (vegetable oils). Second generation are mostly agricultural non-food and agro/urban waste (such as animal fats, used cooking oils and agricultural waste) and the third generation feedstocks are non-agricultural high innovation feedstocks (deriving from algae or waste).

Actual GHG emission. GHG emissions (expressed as CO2eq.) emitted in the past or present and accounted for in the emission inventory. Adaptation to climate change. Process of adjustment of ecological, social or economic systems in response to actual or expected climate impacts, aimed to reduce the vulnerability of communities, regions or activities to climate change.

Asset integrity. The ability of an asset to function effectively and accurately, while safeguarding the well-being of personnel and equipment throughout the asset's lifecycle, from its design phase to its decommissioning.

Average reserve life index. Ratio between the amount of reserves at the end of the year and total production for the year.

Barrel/bbl. Volume unit corresponding to 159 liters. A barrel of oil corresponds to about 0.137 metric tonnes.

Boe (Barrel of Oil Equivalent). Is used as a standard unit measure for oil and natural gas. Effective January 1 st , 2023, Eni has updated the conversion rate of gas produced to 5,232 cubic feet of gas equals 1 barrel of oil.

B2C. Business to Consumer refers to all business relationships between the company and the end customer who purchase gas, electricity or other products and services provided by Plenitude for personal or domestic, business or commercial use.

Carbon credits. Permits or certificates generated on a voluntarily basis through an emission reduction or carbon removal project. One carbon credit corresponds to one metric ton of CO2equivalent.

Carbon dioxide Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS). Reservoir technologies applied to carbon capture and storage (CCS), typically used for large emission sources such as power plant or industrial facilities that use fossil fuels or biomass. Captured CO 2 can be used directly on-site or, alternatively, compressed and transported via pipeline, ship, rail or truck to be used in various applications, or injected into confined geological formations, such as depleted oil and gas fields or saline aquifers.

Carbon Neutrality at 2050. A pillar of Eni's business model defining its decarbonization pathway for processes and energy products by 2050, through the use of available and emerging technological solutions. According to the IPCC definition, Carbon Neutrality describes the condition in which the anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions associated witha subject are balanced by anthropogenic CO 2 removals. The subject can be an entity, such as a country, an organization, a district or a commodity, or an activity such as a service or an event. Carbon Neutrality is often assessed over the full life cycle, including indirect (Scope 3) emissions, but can also be limited to emissions and removals, over a specified period, for which the subject has direct control, as determined by the relevant scheme.

Climate. Statistical description in terms of average and variability of relevant meteorological variables (e.g. temperature, precipitation, winds, etc.), calculated over a period of at least 30 years.

Climate change. A change in the state of the climate that can be identified by changes in the mean and/or the variability of its properties and that persists for an extended period, typically decades or longer. ## Methodological Note

## Scope 1-2

In line with applicable regulatory requirements and consistent with major international standards (WBCSD/WRI GHG Protocol Initiative Standard and sector best practices), GHG emissions are reported for all relevant emission sources, considering the following gases: CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O. Other greenhouse gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF 6 , NF 3 ), based on analysis of available data and in line with Oil & Gas sector practice, are not considered significant as they account for approximately 0.02% of total GHG emissions. Global Warming Potentials (GWPs) from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) over a 100-year horizon are used for conversion into CO2eq.: 29.8 for CH 4 and 273 for N 2 O. Scope 1 GHG emissions are classified into the following categories: (i) Combustion and process (stationary combustion, mobile sources and industrial-process operations); (ii) Flaring (controlled combustion of hydrocarbons via flare); (iii) Venting (controlled release to the atmosphere of unburned gas, mainly CH 4 ,  during operational activities such as Oil & Gas exploration and production, power generation and gas transportation); (iv) Fugitive emissions (unintentional methane leaks from equipment and components such as pumps, valves, compressor seals, etc.). Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions are calculated based on measurement or, where not available, estimation (e.g., fuel consumed, electricity purchased, distance travelled). Depending on their physical origin, data are sourced from: (i) fuel-meter readings; (ii) utility bills (e.g., electricity consumption); (iii) direct measurement (e.g., LDAR campaigns for fugitive emissions); (iv) other methods applied at specific Eni sites and facilities. Emission factors are determined based on gas chemical composition or derived from literature sources. Specifically: (i) for installations subject to the EU ETS, national standard parameters under Regulation (EU) 2018/2066 (updated for 2025) issued by the Ministry for Ecological Transition are applied for natural gas, LPG, refinery fuel gas, petroleum-derived gas and flare gas; (ii) for other installations, the main references are the IPCC guidelines and the API Compendium of Greenhouse Gas Emissions Methodologies for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry (2009/2021) for CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O. At Eni sites where LDAR programmes are in place, fugitive CH 4 emissions are determined using periodic leak-measurement campaigns. Measurement results are used to quantify annual emissions by applying emission factors from API, EPA (e.g., EPA Protocol No. 453) and OGMP standards. At sites where LDAR is not implemented, fugitive emissions are estimated based on equipment-component inventories (valves, flanges, etc.) or on oil and gas production volumes, using standard emission factors (API Compendium). Biogenic CO 2 Scope 1 emissions are reported separately; they amounted to 0.27 and 0.21 MtCO2eq. in 2024 and 2025 respectively, and derive from biomass combustion and biomethane production processes. Scope 2 emissions are reported according to two approaches: a)  Location-Based - based on the average electricity-generation mix of the Country from which third-party electricity is purchased (IEA Emission Factors database); b) Market-Based - based on supplier-specific electricity-data, considering the share of renewable electricity, the Country residual mix, and contractual instruments linked or unlinked to the supply contracts (in 2025, these instruments covered around 55% of total electricity purchases). Emissions associated with non-renewable or non-certified supply are calculated using supplier-specific factors or the residual mix where available; otherwise, the Country electricity mix is used (AIB 2024 factors). Emission factors for steam purchases are derived from the API Compendium. Biogenic CO 2 Scope 2 emissions are not estimated as they are deemed not significant. ## SCENARIO ANALYSIS

The identification of Eni's physical and transition risks is also supported by an in-depth analysis of climate scenarios. At the international level, a wide range of scenarios currently exists, developed by numerous analysts, consultants, organisations and energy-sector entities. These scenarios rely on different construction methodologies and outline a broad spectrum of possible evolutions of the energy system. They combine decarbonisation levers, technologies, assumptions on the evolution of consumption patterns and policy frameworks in different ways, in order to illustrate potential future trajectories and provide a useful reference framework for guiding strategic choices and policy directions. In this context, given the absence of universally recognised decarbonisation pathways for the Oil & Gas sector, Eni  analyses multiple prospective pathways characterised by heterogeneous mixes of solutions and milestones, among which those developed by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) are particularly relevant. Specifically, climate scenarios belonging to the IPCC C1-C2 categories were used as a reference for assessing the compatibility of Eni decarbonisation plan 25  with trajectories aligned with the 1.5°C limit by 2100, while acknowledging the intrinsic limitations of comparing a corporate context with the global one (see Decarbonisation levers ). The IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) scenario was considered for assessing the resilience of Eni's strategy to transition risks (see Resilience of the strategy to transition scenarios ), whereas the IPCC SSP5-RCP8.5 (C8) scenario was used for the analysis of physical risks (see Physical risks ).

## Main reference scenarios

IEA - Net Zero Emissions (NZE) Scenario: in the World Energy Outlook 2025, the IEA revised the assumptions underpinning the NZE scenario (the scenario targeting Net Zero emissions by 2050), shifting from a limited-overshoot pathway to a high-overshoot 26  one. In this scenario - for which the IEA provides numerical detail only at the global level - decarbonisation of the energy system is achieved primarily through increasing electrification and a major scale-up of variable renewables (whose share in the power-generation mix rises from today's 15% to around 75% in 2050), improved energy efficiency, and rapid deployment of CO 2 capture and storage technologies for industrial processes (CCUS), bioenergy with CCS (BECCS) and direct air capture (DACS). In terms of energy mix, the NZE-IEA scenario features a substantial decline in the role of fossil fuels, whose share in the global mix drops from the current 79% to 16% by 2050, alongside a falling energy demand (0.5% per year on average between 2024 and 2050). By 2050, the most affected energy source is coal, with emissions falling by 99% compared with 2024 (consumption down 92%), followed by natural gas (95% emissions; consumption down 80%) and oil (90% emissions; consumption down 77%).

Unlike the IEA, the IPCC develops climate scenarios 27  by considering all GHG emissions, not only CO 2 from the energy sector. These scenarios are grouped into eight categories (C1-C8) 28  based on the projected increase in global temperature by 2100 associated with each pathway. Categories C1 and C2 include over 200 scenarios capable of limiting global warming to 1.5°C: (i) C1 includes scenarios with no or limited overshoot (with Net Zero GHG emissions reached between 2030 and 2100, depending on the scenario); (ii) C2 includes high-overshoot scenarios. The decarbonisation levers and technologies deployed in these pathways, while broadly similar to those of the NZE-IEA scenario, are combined in different ways. For example, electrification in these trajectories does not necessarily rely almost exclusively on variable renewables - it may also derive from an expanded role of nuclear power. ## WATER & WASTE MANAGEMENT

Eni Rewind manages water treatment for the purpose of remediation activities at Eni sites and owned by Eni Rewind, through an integrated system for intercepting the aquifer and conveying groundwater to treatment plants for its purification.

The automation and digitalization project of the treatment plants continued in 2025 as part of a broader optimization initiative, with the aim of increasing the competitiveness and sustainability of the business, the quality of work and process safety.

The main drivers of the project consist in the adoption of optimized operating models for the management of the plants, already operational in some sites, leveraging the enhancement of the Control Room in San Donato Milanese and the digitization of the sites connected to it. A further area of digitization is that of the maintenance process, which has seen the adoption of special maintenance management software service.

Currently, 45 water treatment plants are operational and managed in Italy, with approximately 40 million cubic meters of water treated in 2025, an increase compared to the previous year.

In December 2025, more than about 10 million cubic meters of water were reused after treatment, thanks to higher volumes emitted due to higher rainfall and grater withdrawal of water for industrial use.

Eni Rewind is Eni's center of competence for the management of waste both from reclamation and remediation activities and from Eni's production sites, for which it carries out a specialist waste management service.

Eni Rewind managed a total of about 2.2 million tons of waste in 2025, an increase compared to 2024, sending it for recovery or disposal at external plants. The difference is due to the increase in liquid waste, managed for disposal at external plants, produced by the Upstream business and from Eni's Biorefining division, for the emergency safety measures (MISE) at the Sannazzaro site and for the soils produced in Livorno during the construction works of the Biorefinery.

The recovery index (ratio of recovered/recoverable waste) was 78%, a slight increase compared to 2024 (76%), due to the actual analytical characteristics of the mix of waste managed. Hazardous waste amounts to 21% of the total. Compared to the total volumes managed by Eni Rewind in 2025, the part relating to Eni customers currently makes up about 83% of the total.
